rounds.proof_sketch: With var << eps, inv_std ≈ 1/sqrt(eps). Original: 1/sqrt(1e-5)≈316, Mutant: 1/sqrt(1e-4)=100. For var=1e-6 and (val-mean)≈1e-3: outputs differ by ~0.2, exceeding threshold ~0.013.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutant would only survive if variance always dominated epsilon in the denominator. For typical large-magnitude inputs with substantial variance, both eps values are negligible. However, when input values are scaled to have variance comparable to or smaller than eps (1e-5), the epsilon difference directly impacts inv_std computation by a factor of ~3x, causing large output divergence.
rounds.kill_strategy: Create input with very small variance by using values drawn from N(0, 1e-3). This makes variance ≈ 1e-6, so eps dominates the denominator. The inv_std ratio between original and mutant becomes ~3x, producing output differences of ~0.2 which far exceeds the tolerance threshold.
rounds.recommendations: When testing normalization kernels, always include test cases with near-zero variance inputs to verify epsilon handling. The epsilon parameter is critical for numerical stability and should be tested at boundary conditions.
rounds.suggested_code:
def generate_inputs(device):
    # Create input with very small variance (variance << eps)
    # This makes epsilon dominate the denominator: inv_std = 1/sqrt(var + eps)
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    x = torch.randn(16, 64, 256, 256, device=device, dtype=torch.float32) * 1e-3
    return [x]
